title: Westminster and Downing Street Light Diyas for Diwali With Indian Diaspora
excerpt: The India APPG helped host the annual Westminster Diwali celebration while No. 10 held its diaspora reception, with speakers tying the festival to the UK-India trade deal and Starmer's Mumbai visit.
body:
• Diwali was celebrated at Westminster and at 10 Downing Street this month, with the India All Party Parliamentary Group helping host the annual Westminster gathering alongside the High Commission of India in London.
  • Prime Minister Keir Starmer's Diwali message was read out by Lord Krish Raval at the Westminster celebration.
  • Speakers tied the festival to the UK-India Free Trade Agreement and the recent run of prime ministerial visits between the two countries.
  • For British Indian readers, the gatherings put the 1.8 million-strong community at the centre of the UK-India relationship that ministers called the Living Bridge.

Diyas were lit at Westminster and at 10 Downing Street this month as Britain's political establishment marked Diwali with the Indian diaspora. The annual Westminster celebration was hosted in collaboration with the High Commission of India in London, the India All Party Parliamentary Group, the British Indian think tank 1928 Institute and the India Global Forum, according to PTI.

Prime Minister Keir Starmer's Diwali message was read out at the Westminster gathering by British Indian peer Lord Krish Raval. India APPG co-chair Lord Karan Bilimoria and president Baroness Sandy Verma were among those who flagged the bilateral partnership, boosted by the signing of the Free Trade Agreement and back-to-back prime ministerial visits. The India APPG is a cross-party group of MPs and peers whose stated purpose includes trade, culture and people-to-people links between the UK and India.

Last year's Downing Street reception

The No. 10 reception is a fixture of the season in its own right. At last year's, held in October 2025, Communities Secretary Steve Reed hosted on behalf of Starmer, who was in Egypt for the Gaza summit, Asian Voice reported. Reed lit diyas at an entrance hall decorated with marigold flowers, candles, diyas and rangolis, and guests were served vegetarian canapes including bhindi jaipuri and mini aloo tikki burgers.

"I believe the message of Diwali, light overcoming darkness, of hope and unity resonates all the more deeply with so many of us at this particular moment in the planet's history."

— Steve Reed, Secretary of State for Communities

More than 100 guests attended that reception, including MPs, peers, councillors, high commissioners, community leaders, members of the armed forces and representatives of temples and community organisations, according to Asian Voice. Prayers were recited by Visakha Dasi of Bhaktivedanta Manor, and Chinmaya Swaranjali performed the Hanuman Chalisa.

The Mumbai visit and the trade deal

Seema Malhotra, Minister for Equalities and the Indo-Pacific, set the scene at the 2025 reception. "The bonds between Britain and India are woven through families like ours," she said, adding that those bonds were renewed and strengthened by Starmer's visit to India earlier that month. She described the Indian diaspora as the Living Bridge between the two nations.

https://x.com/themworldnews/status/2112984243760701789

Secretary of State for Scotland Douglas Alexander, who travelled to India with the 127-strong prime ministerial delegation in October 2025, said the Mumbai visit focused on putting the trade deal agreed the previous July to work. "It was very striking that India is a superpower in the making," Alexander said. "This visit felt generationally significant, pregnant with possibilities for the future." He pointed to the 1.8 million British citizens of Indian heritage as central to what the partnership can do next.

Indian High Commissioner Vikram Doraiswami told the Westminster gathering that Diwali was a moment to take stock. "Diwali is an opportunity for us to take stock of the year that was, and to look ahead at the year that will be, and the year that will be in the India-UK context, I'm convinced is a great one," he said. He said the work ahead was to see how business, education partnerships and technology partnerships can contribute to growth in both countries.

What it means for the diaspora

For British Indians, the Westminster celebration and the No. 10 reception tradition are the public face of a relationship now being driven by the Free Trade Agreement and the follow-up to Starmer's October 2025 India visit. Kanishka Narayan, the Bihar-born Minister for AI and Online Safety, told the Westminster celebration that moments like Diwali allow the community to celebrate that relationship in personal terms, PTI reported.

What happens next

The focus now shifts from celebration to implementation: ministers at both events said the trade deal must be used by businesses, universities and technology firms rather than left on the shelf. London's wider Diwali season continues in public spaces across the capital in the run-up to the festival.
